claims.text: Catalytic selectivity of transition-metal catalysts is governed by the surface oxidation state of the metal sites.
Surface oxidation state may also govern catalytic activity.
Surface oxidation state may also govern catalyst durability.
Modifying the surface oxidation state alters the electronic structure, including the d-band center, of active sites.
Changes in the d-band center adjust the adsorption energies of reaction intermediates.
Changes in intermediate adsorption energies control the reaction pathway and catalytic selectivity.
A controlled oxidation or reduction treatment will adjust the catalyst's surface oxidation state.
The controlled comparison should keep particle size and support morphology constant while varying redox treatment.
The treated and untreated catalysts should be tested under identical catalytic reaction conditions.
A redox-treated catalyst will exhibit a measurable selectivity shift relative to the untreated catalyst.
The proposed relationship should hold only over a limited range of oxidation-state modification in which catalyst structural integrity is maintained.
The magnitude of the performance change depends on the specific reaction and catalyst system.
XPS should be used to verify that the redox treatment changed the surface oxidation state.
The hypothesis is falsified if a verified oxidation-state modification produces no statistically significant selectivity change relative to the untreated control.
The hypothesis is falsified if observed performance changes do not correlate with the verified surface oxidation-state modification.
